title: “I Am a Ghost”
author: Satyajit Ray
raw_text:
Chapter 1 “I Am a Ghost” by Satyajit Ray 
“I Am a Ghost” is a humorous yet touching supernatural short story by Satyajit Ray. Unlike 
traditional ghost stories that aim to frighten readers, this story is narrated by a ghost himself and 
focuses on loneliness, friendship, morality, and the desire for companionship. The story was first 
published in 1985 and later included in collections of Ray’s supernatural tales. 
Introduction: The Ghost Narrator 
The story begins with an unusual declaration: “I am a ghost.” The narrator introduces himself as 
Sudhanya, a man who died three years earlier in a tragic accident at a house called Lily Villa in 
Deoghar. While preparing tea during a holiday stay, a gas stove exploded, setting his clothes on fire 
and causing his death. Since then, he has existed as a ghost in the same house. 
Sudhanya explains that although he is a ghost, he is not evil or dangerous. He can make himself 
visible or invisible at will, but he usually remains unseen because he does not want to frighten 
people. His ghostly appearance, especially his burnt face, can be terrifying to humans. 
Life as a Lonely Ghost 
Sudhanya spends his days wandering around Lily Villa. One day, while absent-mindedly looking out 
of a window, he accidentally becomes visible to a family visiting the house. The sight of his burnt face 
terrifies them. The head of the family faints, and the family immediately leaves. 
News spreads quickly that Lily Villa is haunted. As a result, nobody is willing to rent or stay in the 
house anymore. What seems amusing at first soon becomes a problem for Sudhanya. He becomes 
extremely lonely because no human visitors come near the villa. 
The loneliness of ghostly existence becomes one of the central themes of the story. Sudhanya misses 
conversation and human company. Although he is dead, he still possesses human emotions and 
desires companionship. 
Other Ghosts and Their Behaviour 
Sudhanya tells readers about the world of ghosts. He explains that not all ghosts are alike. Some are 
harmless, while others are mischievous or even cruel. 
Among these spirits is a notorious ghost named Naskar-da, whom Sudhanya strongly dislikes. 
Naskar-da enjoys interfering in human affairs and causing trouble. Sudhanya believes ghosts should 
not meddle with the lives of living people. 
To illustrate Naskar-da's wickedness, Sudhanya narrates an incident involving a postmaster named 
Lakshman Tripathi and a bank employee named Kantibhai Dubey. Through manipulation and 
mischief, Naskar-da causes a tragedy in which an innocent man is blamed and punished. This episode 
highlights the moral difference between Sudhanya and Naskar-da. While one ghost respects 
humanity, the other exploits it. 
Arrival of Narayan Sharma 
The story takes a dramatic turn when a famous writer and researcher named Narayan Sharma 
arrives at Lily Villa. Sharma is deeply interested in ghosts, spirits, and supernatural phenomena. He 

chooses to stay in the haunted house because he hopes to study ghosts and gather material for his 
writings. 
For Sudhanya, Sharma's arrival is exciting. After years of loneliness, he finally has a human 
companion in the house. He watches the writer closely and hopes to establish some kind of 
connection. 
However, Sudhanya soon discovers that Sharma has unusual plans. The writer is not merely studying 
ghosts; he wants to experiment with methods of controlling or frightening them. 
The Ghost-Hunting Experiment 
Narayan Sharma prepares a mysterious powder that, when burned, releases a special smoke. 
According to Sharma's research, this smoke has the power to affect ghosts. 
When Sharma burns the powder, Sudhanya finds himself unable to resist its effects. The smoke 
makes him drowsy, and eventually he falls into a deep sleep. 
This part of the story combines humour and fantasy. The idea that a ghost can be put to sleep by 
scientific experimentation turns traditional ghost stories upside down. Instead of ghosts frightening 
humans, a human appears capable of controlling ghosts. 
The Unexpected Twist 
When Sudhanya finally wakes up, he notices something strange. Narayan Sharma is no longer alive. 
Sharma reveals that while making tea, he experienced the same fate as Sudhanya. A gas stove 
explosion caused his death. Now he, too, has become a ghost. 
This revelation forms the story's ironic and humorous climax. The man who came to study ghosts 
has become one himself. 
Conclusion: Friendship Beyond Death 
The story ends on a warm and optimistic note. Sudhanya is no longer alone. Narayan Sharma, now a 
ghost, becomes his companion. 
The ending transforms what could have been a horror story into a tale about friendship and 
understanding. Both ghosts can now share their experiences and keep each other company. The 
loneliness that haunted Sudhanya throughout the story is finally overcome. 
Critical Appreciation 
“I Am a Ghost” is a unique ghost story because it replaces horror with empathy. Satyajit Ray uses 
humour, irony, and a first-person ghost narrator to challenge conventional ideas about ghosts. The 
story reminds readers that emotions such as loneliness, kindness, and the desire for friendship 
transcend even death. Its memorable ending and compassionate portrayal of the supernatural make 
it one of Ray's most engaging and thought-provoking tales. 
I Am a Ghost by Satyajit Ray – Question Bank with Answers 
Part A: 2-Mark Questions and Answers 

1. Who is the narrator of the story I Am a Ghost? 
Answer: The narrator is Sudhanya, a ghost who lives in Lily Villa after his death in a gas stove 
explosion. 
2. How did Sudhanya die? 
Answer: Sudhanya died when a gas stove exploded while he was making tea, causing severe 
burns. 
3. Where does Sudhanya live after his death? 
Answer: He continues to live as a ghost in Lily Villa, a house in Deoghar. 
4. Why do people avoid Lily Villa? 
Answer: People avoid Lily Villa because they believe it is haunted after seeing Sudhanya's 
ghostly appearance. 
5. Who is Naskar-da? 
Answer: Naskar-da is another ghost who enjoys creating trouble and interfering in human 
affairs. 
6. What kind of ghost is Sudhanya? 
Answer: Sudhanya is a kind, harmless, and friendly ghost who does not wish to frighten 
people. 
7. Who is Narayan Sharma? 
Answer: Narayan Sharma is a writer and researcher interested in studying ghosts and 
supernatural phenomena. 
8. Why does Narayan Sharma stay at Lily Villa? 
Answer: He stays there to investigate and learn about ghosts. 
9. What experiment does Narayan Sharma conduct? 
Answer: He burns a special powder that produces smoke believed to affect ghosts. 
10. How does the story end? 
Answer: Narayan Sharma dies in a gas stove explosion and becomes a ghost, becoming 
Sudhanya's companion. 
Part B: 5-Mark Questions and Answers 
1. Describe the character of Sudhanya. 
Answer: Sudhanya is the protagonist and narrator of the story. He became a ghost after dying 
in a gas stove explosion. Unlike traditional ghosts, he is kind-hearted, gentle, and considerate. 
He does not enjoy frightening people and prefers to remain invisible. He suffers from 
loneliness because people avoid Lily Villa after learning it is haunted. His longing for 
companionship reveals his human emotions. Sudhanya's goodness is contrasted with the 
mischievous ghost Naskar-da, making him a sympathetic and memorable character. 
2. Explain the significance of Lily Villa in the story. 
Answer: Lily Villa serves as the main setting of the story. It is the place where Sudhanya died 
and where he continues to live as a ghost. The villa symbolizes isolation and loneliness 
because people stop visiting it after hearing stories about ghosts. At the same time, it becomes 

the place where Sudhanya finally finds companionship through Narayan Sharma. Thus, Lily 
Villa represents both loneliness and friendship. 
3. How is Naskar-da different from Sudhanya? 
Answer: Naskar-da and Sudhanya represent two different kinds of ghosts. Sudhanya is kind, 
compassionate, and avoids interfering in human lives. Naskar-da, however, enjoys creating 
confusion and causing suffering among people. He takes pleasure in mischief and 
manipulation. Through these contrasting characters, Satyajit Ray shows that moral qualities 
remain important even after death. 
4. Describe the role of Narayan Sharma in the story. 
Answer: Narayan Sharma is a writer and ghost researcher who comes to Lily Villa to study 
supernatural phenomena. His arrival brings excitement to Sudhanya, who has been lonely for 
years. Sharma conducts experiments to understand ghosts and unknowingly affects Sudhanya 
with a special smoke. Ironically, Sharma later dies in the same manner as Sudhanya and 
becomes a ghost himself. His transformation provides the story's humorous and unexpected 
ending. 
5. Discuss the theme of loneliness in I Am a Ghost. 
Answer: Loneliness is one of the central themes of the story. After becoming a ghost, Sudhanya 
is isolated because people are afraid of him. Even though he is harmless, his appearance scares 
visitors away. He longs for human interaction and companionship. His happiness at gaining 
Narayan Sharma as a fellow ghost demonstrates the importance of friendship and emotional 
connection. Ray shows that loneliness can affect both the living and the dead. 
Part C: Essay Questions and Answers 
1. Discuss I Am a Ghost as a humorous ghost story. 
Answer: 
Satyajit Ray's I Am a Ghost is a unique ghost story because it combines supernatural elements 
with humour. Unlike conventional ghost stories that focus on fear and horror, this story 
presents a ghost as the narrator and portrays him as a friendly, lonely individual. 
The narrator, Sudhanya, explains how he died and became a ghost. Instead of terrorizing 
people, he tries to avoid frightening them. His accidental appearance scares visitors away, 
leaving him lonely. This reversal of traditional ghost-story expectations creates humour. 
Another humorous aspect is the character of Narayan Sharma, a writer determined to study 
ghosts scientifically. He attempts to control ghosts through experiments. However, in a twist of 
irony, he dies in a gas stove explosion and becomes a ghost himself. The ghost hunter 
becoming a ghost is both amusing and unexpected. 
Ray uses irony, wit, and gentle satire to challenge readers' assumptions about ghosts. The 
story remains entertaining while also conveying meaningful themes about friendship and 
loneliness. Thus, I Am a Ghost can be considered a humorous and unconventional ghost story. 
2. Examine the major themes in I Am a Ghost. 
Answer: 
Satyajit Ray's I Am a Ghost explores several important themes. 

Loneliness 
Sudhanya's greatest problem is not death but isolation. People avoid Lily Villa because they 
fear ghosts, leaving him without companionship. 
Friendship and Companionship 
The story emphasizes the importance of friendship. Sudhanya's loneliness ends when Narayan 
Sharma becomes a ghost and joins him. 
Morality 
Through Sudhanya and Naskar-da, Ray shows that good and bad qualities continue even after 
death. Sudhanya is compassionate, while Naskar-da is mischievous. 
Irony 
The story contains a strong sense of irony. Narayan Sharma comes to investigate ghosts but 
eventually becomes one himself. 
Humanizing the Supernatural 
Ray presents ghosts as emotional beings capable of kindness, loneliness, and friendship. This 
humanized portrayal makes readers sympathize with Sudhanya rather than fear him. 
These themes make the story both entertaining and thought-provoking. 
3. Analyze the character of Sudhanya in I Am a Ghost. 
Answer: 
Sudhanya is the central character and narrator of I Am a Ghost. His character is unusual 
because he is a ghost who behaves more humanely than many living people. 
Before his death, Sudhanya was an ordinary man. A tragic gas stove explosion transformed 
him into a ghost. Despite his frightening appearance, he remains kind and gentle. He dislikes 
causing fear and prefers to stay invisible. His actions reveal a thoughtful and caring 
personality. 
Sudhanya suffers greatly from loneliness. Since people avoid Lily Villa, he has no one to talk to. 
His emotional pain makes him a sympathetic figure. His interactions with Naskar-da further 
highlight his moral nature. While Naskar-da enjoys creating trouble, Sudhanya respects 
human beings and avoids harming them. 
The arrival of Narayan Sharma gives Sudhanya hope. By the end of the story, he gains a 
companion, bringing happiness to his otherwise lonely existence. 
Sudhanya symbolizes the idea that humanity is defined by character rather than physical form. 
Through him, Satyajit Ray creates a memorable and lovable ghost who challenges traditional 
stereotypes about supernatural beings.

author: W. Somerset Maugham

Chapter 2 The Verger by W. Somerset Maugham 
The Verger is a humorous and ironic short story by W. Somerset Maugham that explores themes of 
self-worth, dignity, education, social prejudice, and the unexpected paths to success. The story 
centers on Albert Edward Foreman, a proud and efficient verger who has faithfully served St. Peter’s 
Church in Neville Square, London, for sixteen years. Foreman takes immense pride in his work and 
appearance, always dressed immaculately in his official verger’s gown, which symbolizes his identity 
and social standing. He performs all his duties with exceptional dedication, maintaining the church, 
assisting during services, and ensuring that everything runs smoothly. Although he has never 
learned to read or write, his practical intelligence, experience, and sense of responsibility make him 
highly respected by the parishioners and clergy. His illiteracy has never interfered with his ability to 
carry out his responsibilities effectively, and no one had previously considered it a serious issue. 
The story begins shortly after a christening ceremony when the newly appointed vicar asks Foreman 
to meet him in the vestry. Present during the meeting are the churchwardens, who support the 
vicar’s concerns. The new vicar, unlike his easy-going predecessor, believes that every church official 
should be literate. During the conversation, Foreman calmly admits that he cannot read or write and 
explains that he was forced to leave school at an early age to earn a living. The previous vicar had 
known about his illiteracy but had never considered it a problem because Foreman had always 
performed his duties perfectly. However, the new vicar insists that such ignorance is unacceptable 
in modern times. He gives Foreman three months to learn reading and writing, warning that if he 
fails, he must resign from his position. Foreman politely but firmly refuses to learn, stating that he is 
too old to begin studying and has managed well throughout his life without literacy. Consequently, 
he loses the job that had been central to his identity for many years. 
Deeply saddened by his dismissal, Foreman leaves the church and begins walking through unfamiliar 
streets without any particular destination. While reflecting on his uncertain future, he suddenly feels 
the desire to smoke a cigarette. Looking around, he realizes that there is no tobacco shop in the entire 
neighbourhood. His practical mind immediately recognizes this as a business opportunity. He 
reasons that if he wants cigarettes, many others probably do as well. Inspired by this simple 
observation, he uses his savings to open a small tobacconist's shop that also sells newspapers, 
sweets, and other everyday items. The business quickly becomes successful because there is genuine 
local demand. Encouraged by his profits, Foreman gradually opens more tobacco shops across 
London. His natural business instincts, careful management, honesty, and dedication enable him to 
build a thriving commercial enterprise. Over the years, he becomes a wealthy and respected 
businessman, employing many people and earning an impressive income despite remaining 
illiterate. 
Eventually, Foreman visits his bank to deposit the substantial profits from his businesses. The bank 
manager is astonished by the amount of money Foreman has accumulated and suggests that he 
invest it in stocks and securities to earn even greater returns. While discussing the necessary 
paperwork, the manager discovers that Foreman cannot read or write. Shocked, he remarks that it 
is extraordinary that an illiterate man has built such a successful business empire. He then asks 
Foreman what he might have become if he had been educated. Foreman smiles and delivers the 
story’s memorable final line: “I know very well what I’d be. I’d be verger of St. Peter’s, Neville Square.” 
This ironic conclusion highlights the central message of the story. Ironically, the very limitation that 

caused Foreman to lose his respectable church position became the reason he discovered his 
entrepreneurial talent and achieved far greater financial success. Had he remained employed as the 
church verger, he would never have entered business or realized his full potential. 
The story illustrates that formal education, while valuable, is not the only measure of intelligence or 
capability. Through Albert Edward Foreman, Maugham emphasizes the importance of practical 
wisdom, observation, perseverance, confidence, and the ability to recognize opportunities. 
Foreman’s success is built not on academic qualifications but on discipline, integrity, sound 
judgment, and hard work. The story also critiques social attitudes that judge people solely by 
educational standards, suggesting that character, competence, and experience are equally 
important. With its subtle humour, realistic characterization, and ironic ending, The Verger remains 
a powerful reminder that success can emerge from unexpected circumstances and that adversity 
often opens doors to greater opportunities.

Part A: Two-Mark Questions (2 Marks Each) 
1. Who is the protagonist of The Verger? 
Answer: The protagonist is Albert Edward Foreman, the verger of St. Peter's Church, Neville 
Square. He is hardworking, dignified, and respected despite being illiterate. 
2. What is the role of a verger? 
Answer: A verger is a church official responsible for maintaining the church, preparing it for 
services, assisting the clergy, and ensuring everything runs smoothly during religious 
ceremonies. 
3. Why does the new vicar dismiss Foreman? 
Answer: The new vicar dismisses Foreman because he cannot read or write and refuses to 
learn within the three months given to him. 
4. How long had Foreman served as the verger? 
Answer: Foreman had served as the verger of St. Peter's Church for sixteen years. 
5. Why had Foreman never learned to read or write? 
Answer: Foreman had to leave school at an early age to earn a living and therefore never 
received a proper education. 
6. What business does Foreman start? 
Answer: Foreman opens a tobacco and newspaper shop, which later grows into a chain of 
successful tobacco shops. 
7. What inspires Foreman to open a tobacco shop? 
Answer: While walking after losing his job, Foreman wants a cigarette but cannot find a 
tobacco shop in the area, which inspires him to open one. 

8. What surprises the bank manager? 
Answer: The bank manager is surprised that Foreman has become wealthy despite being 
unable to read or write. 
9. What is the irony at the end of the story? 
Answer: The irony is that losing his job because of illiteracy ultimately leads Foreman to 
become a wealthy businessman. 
10. Mention one theme of the story. 
Answer: One important theme is that practical intelligence and determination can be as 
valuable as formal education. 
Part B: Five-Mark Questions (5 Marks Each) 
1. Character Sketch of Albert Edward Foreman. 
Answer: 
Albert Edward Foreman is the central character of the story. He is hardworking, disciplined, 
honest, and takes immense pride in his work as the church verger. Although he is illiterate, he 
possesses practical intelligence and excellent organizational skills. He performs his duties with 
dedication and earns the respect of the congregation. When he loses his job, he does not 
complain or blame others. Instead, he turns adversity into opportunity by opening a tobacco 
shop. His determination, business sense, and perseverance make him a successful 
entrepreneur. Foreman proves that intelligence is not limited to formal education. 
2. Why is Foreman dismissed from his job? 
Answer: 
Foreman is dismissed because the newly appointed vicar believes that every church official 
should be educated. During a meeting with the churchwardens, Foreman admits that he 
cannot read or write. Although the previous vicar accepted this fact because Foreman 
performed his duties efficiently, the new vicar insists that literacy is essential. He gives 
Foreman three months to learn reading and writing. However, Foreman refuses, believing he 
is too old to start learning. As a result, he is forced to resign from his position. 
3. Describe how Foreman became a successful businessman. 
Answer: 
After losing his job, Foreman walks through the streets thinking about his future. When he 
cannot find a tobacco shop to buy cigarettes, he notices a business opportunity. He uses his 
savings to open a small tobacco shop, which becomes very successful because there is no 
competition nearby. Gradually, he opens more shops across London. Through hard work, 
honesty, careful management, and practical wisdom, he builds a prosperous business empire. 
His success demonstrates that observation and determination can lead to great achievements. 
4. Explain the irony in the story. 
Answer: 

Irony is the most significant literary device in The Verger. Foreman loses his respected church 
position because he is illiterate. However, that unfortunate event leads him to discover his 
talent for business. Instead of remaining an ordinary church employee, he becomes a wealthy 
businessman. At the end, when the bank manager says that Foreman could have become an 
important man if he had been educated, Foreman humorously replies that he would simply 
have remained the verger of St. Peter's Church. Thus, the very weakness that cost him his job 
becomes the reason for his success. 
5. Discuss the themes of the story. 
Answer: 
The story presents several important themes. The most important theme is that practical 
intelligence is often more valuable than formal education. Another theme is perseverance, as 
Foreman refuses to let failure defeat him. The story also highlights dignity of labour, showing 
that every job deserves respect. Social prejudice is another theme because the new vicar 
judges Foreman solely on the basis of his illiteracy. Finally, the story emphasizes that failure 
can become the beginning of success if one recognizes opportunities. 
Part C: Essay Questions (10–15 Marks) 
1. Discuss The Verger as a story of irony and success. 
Answer: 
The Verger is an excellent example of irony because the central conflict and the ending are 
based on unexpected outcomes. Albert Edward Foreman is a devoted church verger who 
performs his duties efficiently despite being unable to read or write. The previous vicar 
appreciates his sincerity and experience, but the new vicar believes that literacy is essential 
for all church officials. As a result, Foreman loses his job. 
Although this appears to be a tragedy, it becomes the turning point of his life. While walking 
through the streets after his dismissal, Foreman notices that there is no tobacco shop nearby. 
This simple observation inspires him to open one. The business flourishes, and over time he 
expands it into a chain of shops across London. He becomes financially successful and highly 
respected. 
The greatest irony appears at the end when the bank manager discovers that Foreman is 
illiterate. Amazed by his success, the manager remarks that Foreman could have become an 
even greater man if he had received an education. Foreman replies that if he had been 
educated, he would still be the verger of St. Peter's Church. This witty statement highlights the 
irony that losing his job led him to a far better life. 
The story teaches that setbacks can become opportunities and that success depends not only 
on education but also on determination, observation, confidence, and practical wisdom. 
2. Analyse the character of Albert Edward Foreman. 
Answer: 
Albert Edward Foreman is one of W. Somerset Maugham's most memorable characters. He is a 
man of dignity, honesty, discipline, and practical intelligence. Even though he lacks formal 

education, he performs his responsibilities with remarkable efficiency. He is respected by the 
church congregation because of his neat appearance, reliability, and commitment. 
When the new vicar dismisses him due to his illiteracy, Foreman remains calm and accepts the 
decision without bitterness. His ability to remain composed reflects his maturity and self-
respect. Rather than depending on others, he chooses to create his own future. 
Foreman's greatest strength is his practical intelligence. He identifies a business opportunity 
where others see nothing unusual. His careful planning, honesty, and hard work enable him to 
establish a successful chain of tobacco shops. Despite becoming wealthy, he remains humble 
and modest. 
Foreman demonstrates that success depends on qualities such as determination, common 
sense, perseverance, and integrity rather than academic qualifications alone. He is an inspiring 
example of resilience and self-confidence. 
3. "Practical intelligence is more important than formal education." Discuss with reference to The 
Verger. 
Answer: 
The Verger strongly suggests that practical intelligence can be as valuable as formal education. 
Albert Edward Foreman cannot read or write, yet he performs his duties as a church verger 
with great efficiency. His dedication earns him respect from everyone except the new vicar, 
who believes that literacy alone determines competence. 
After being dismissed, Foreman uses his practical knowledge and powers of observation to 
identify a business opportunity. He notices that there is no tobacco shop in a busy 
neighbourhood and opens one. His business grows rapidly because he understands customers' 
needs and manages his shops wisely. 
The story does not argue that education is unimportant. Instead, it shows that education alone 
does not guarantee success. Practical intelligence, sound judgment, hard work, honesty, and 
perseverance are equally important. Foreman's achievements demonstrate that people should 
not be judged solely by their educational qualifications. 
Through humour and irony, Maugham encourages readers to value experience and common 
sense alongside formal learning. The story remains relevant because it reminds us that success 
comes in many forms and that talent can exist outside the classroom.

title: A Letter to God
author: Gregorio López y Fuentes

Chapter 3 A Letter to God by Gregorio López y Fuentes 
A Letter to God is a touching and inspiring short story by Gregorio López y Fuentes that highlights 
the themes of faith, hope, human kindness, irony, and the resilience of the human spirit. The story 
revolves around Lencho, a poor but hardworking farmer who lives with his family in a small house 
on the crest of a hill. His entire livelihood depends on the success of his corn and bean crops. At the 
beginning of the story, Lencho eagerly looks forward to rainfall because his fields need water for a 
good harvest. Dark clouds gather, and the first drops of rain fill him with joy as he believes that 
nature is blessing his crops. However, his happiness is short-lived when the rain suddenly turns into 
a violent hailstorm. Huge hailstones fall relentlessly, destroying the fields, flattening the crops, and 
leaving the land completely devastated. By the time the storm ends, every stalk of corn and every 
bean plant has been ruined. Lencho realizes that his family now faces starvation because they have 
no harvest and no source of income. 
Despite this terrible disaster, Lencho never loses faith in God. He firmly believes that God sees 
everything and will surely help those who trust Him. Convinced that divine help will come, Lencho 
decides to write a letter to God. In the letter, he explains his misfortune and asks for one hundred 
pesos, the amount he believes is necessary to sow his fields again and feed his family until the next 
harvest. He addresses the envelope simply to “God” and posts it without any doubt that it will reach 
its destination. 
When the letter arrives at the post office, the postmaster is amazed by Lencho's extraordinary faith. 
Deeply moved and unwilling to let such faith be disappointed, he decides to answer the letter. He 
laughs at first but soon realizes that he must do something worthy of Lencho's trust. The postmaster 
contributes part of his own salary and persuades his colleagues and friends to donate money as well. 
Although they cannot collect the full amount requested, they manage to raise seventy pesos. The 
postmaster places the money in an envelope, signs it “God,” and sends it to Lencho. 
Lencho receives the envelope with complete confidence, expecting God's assistance. He is not 
surprised that God has answered his request because his faith is absolute. However, when he counts 
the money, he finds only seventy pesos instead of the one hundred he had requested. Rather than 
doubting God, Lencho concludes that God could never make a mistake or send less than the required 
amount. Instead, he believes that the missing thirty pesos must have been stolen by the employees 
at the post office. Angered by this thought, he writes another letter to God requesting the remaining 
thirty pesos. In this second letter, he asks God not to send the money through the mail because, 
according to him, the post office employees are “a bunch of crooks.” 
The story ends with a powerful touch of dramatic irony. The readers know that the post office 
employees are actually generous and compassionate people who sacrificed their own money to help 
Lencho. Ironically, the very people who tried to preserve his faith are accused of dishonesty. This 
ending reveals both the strength and the simplicity of Lencho's faith. His belief in God is so complete 
that he cannot imagine God failing him; instead, he suspects human beings. Through this ironic 
conclusion, the author explores the relationship between faith and human nature, showing how acts 
of kindness often go unnoticed while unwavering faith can remain untouched by hardship. The story 
ultimately teaches that hope, compassion, and generosity can shine even in difficult circumstances, 
and that true faith gives people the courage to face life's greatest challenges. 

A Letter to God by Gregorio López y Fuentes 
2 Marks, 5 Marks, and Essay Questions with Answers 
Part A: Two-Mark Questions (2 Marks Each) 
1. Who is the author of A Letter to God? 
Answer: A Letter to God is written by Gregorio López y Fuentes, a renowned Mexican novelist 
known for portraying the lives of ordinary rural people. 
2. Who is the protagonist of the story? 
Answer: The protagonist is Lencho, a poor but hardworking farmer who has complete faith in 
God. 
3. Where did Lencho live? 
Answer: Lencho lived with his family in a small house on the crest of a hill, surrounded by his 
corn and bean fields. 
4. Why was Lencho eagerly waiting for rain? 
Answer: Lencho was waiting for rain because his crops needed water for a good harvest, and 
his family's livelihood depended entirely on agriculture. 
5. What destroyed Lencho's crops? 
Answer: A severe hailstorm destroyed all of Lencho's corn and bean crops. 
6. Why did Lencho write a letter to God? 
Answer: Lencho wrote a letter asking God for one hundred pesos to help him sow his fields 
again and support his family until the next harvest. 
7. How much money did the postmaster collect? 
Answer: The postmaster and his colleagues managed to collect seventy pesos. 
8. Why was the postmaster impressed by Lencho? 
Answer: The postmaster was impressed by Lencho's unwavering faith in God and wanted to 
preserve that faith. 
9. Why did Lencho call the post office employees "a bunch of crooks"? 
Answer: Lencho believed the post office employees had stolen the missing thirty pesos 
because he thought God would never send less money than requested. 
10. Mention one major theme of the story. 
Answer: One major theme is faith in God. Other themes include hope, kindness, generosity, 
and irony. 
Part B: Five-Mark Questions (5 Marks Each) 
1. Character Sketch of Lencho. 
Answer: 
Lencho is a poor, hardworking, and honest farmer whose life depends entirely on his crops. He 
is deeply religious and possesses unwavering faith in God. Even after losing his entire harvest 

in a hailstorm, he never loses hope. Instead of becoming discouraged, he writes directly to 
God, believing that God will certainly help him. Lencho is also simple and innocent. His 
absolute faith prevents him from believing that God could make a mistake. Therefore, when he 
receives only seventy pesos, he wrongly suspects the post office employees of stealing the 
remaining money. Lencho represents faith, perseverance, and hope in the face of adversity. 
2. Describe the destruction caused by the hailstorm. 
Answer: 
The hailstorm completely destroys Lencho's crops. At first, the rain brings happiness because 
it promises a good harvest. However, the rain soon turns into a violent hailstorm with large 
hailstones falling continuously. The corn fields are flattened, the bean plants are ruined, and 
the land looks as though it has been covered with salt. By the end of the storm, there is nothing 
left to harvest. Lencho realizes that his family faces hunger and poverty because their only 
source of income has been destroyed. 
3. Explain the role of the postmaster in the story. 
Answer: 
The postmaster plays a vital role in the story. When he reads Lencho's letter addressed to God, 
he is amazed by the farmer's faith. Rather than laughing at him, he decides to help preserve 
that faith. He contributes part of his own salary and persuades his colleagues and friends to 
donate money. Although they collect only seventy pesos instead of one hundred, they send the 
money anonymously, signing the letter as "God." The postmaster symbolizes kindness, 
compassion, and generosity. 
4. Explain the irony in the story. 
Answer: 
The story contains dramatic irony because the readers know something that Lencho does not. 
The post office employees sacrifice their own money to help him, but Lencho believes they 
have stolen part of God's gift. Instead of thanking them, he calls them "a bunch of crooks." The 
irony lies in the fact that the people who help him are wrongly accused of dishonesty. This 
ironic ending makes the story humorous while emphasizing the power of Lencho's faith. 
5. Discuss the themes of A Letter to God. 
Answer: 
The story explores several important themes. The most significant theme is faith, as Lencho 
trusts God completely even after losing everything. Another theme is hope, since Lencho 
never gives up despite the disaster. The story also highlights human kindness and 
generosity through the actions of the postmaster and his colleagues. Finally, the theme of 
irony is central because Lencho misunderstands the source of the money and accuses his 
benefactors instead of appreciating them.

1. Discuss A Letter to God as a story of faith and human kindness. 
Answer: 
A Letter to God is a beautiful story that celebrates faith and human compassion. The 
protagonist, Lencho, is a poor farmer whose livelihood depends entirely on his crops. When a 
devastating hailstorm destroys his harvest, he faces starvation and financial ruin. Despite this 
disaster, Lencho does not lose faith in God. He believes that God will never abandon him and 
writes a letter asking for one hundred pesos to support his family and sow his fields again. 
The postmaster, upon reading the letter, is deeply moved by Lencho's faith. He wishes to 
ensure that such trust remains unbroken. He donates part of his salary and collects money

anonymously in God's name. 
Ironically, Lencho is disappointed because the amount is less than what he requested. Since he 
believes God cannot make mistakes, he concludes that the post office employees stole the 
remaining thirty pesos. This misunderstanding creates the story's dramatic irony. 
The story shows that faith can provide hope during difficult times. It also teaches that human 
beings can become instruments of God's kindness through acts of generosity. The postmaster's 
compassion contrasts with Lencho's mistaken suspicion, making the ending both humorous 
and thought-provoking. 
2. Analyse the character of Lencho. 
Answer: 
Lencho is the central character of A Letter to God. He is a hardworking farmer who depends 
entirely on agriculture for his family's survival. His greatest quality is his absolute faith in God. 
Even after losing his crops in a devastating hailstorm, he never complains against God or loses 
hope. Instead, he confidently writes a letter asking for financial assistance. 
Lencho is honest, sincere, and determined. His faith is childlike and unconditional. He believes 
that God sees everything and will certainly answer his prayer. However, his simplicity also 
makes him somewhat naïve. When he receives only seventy pesos instead of one hundred, he 
cannot imagine that God would send less money. Therefore, he wrongly blames the post office 
employees for stealing the rest. 
Lencho represents unwavering faith and perseverance, but he also illustrates how blind trust 
can lead to misunderstanding. Despite his mistake, he remains an unforgettable literary 
character because of his optimism and resilience. 
3. Discuss the themes and literary devices used in A Letter to God. 
Answer: 
A Letter to God explores several universal themes through simple language and an engaging 
narrative. The primary theme is faith in God. Lencho never doubts God's power, even after 
suffering a great loss. The story also emphasizes hope, showing that faith helps people endure 
hardship. 

Another important theme is human kindness. The postmaster and his colleagues willingly 
contribute money to help a stranger. Their generosity demonstrates compassion and 
selflessness. The theme of irony dominates the conclusion. Readers know that the post office 
employees are the real benefactors, but Lencho believes they have stolen from him. 
The author effectively uses dramatic irony, where readers know more than the main 
character. Characterization portrays Lencho as faithful and innocent, while the postmaster 
represents kindness and empathy. Symbolism is also present: the hailstorm symbolizes life's 
unexpected hardships, while the letter symbolizes hope and unwavering belief. 
Through these themes and literary techniques, the story teaches that faith, generosity, and 
resilience are essential qualities that help people overcome adversity.

Chapter 4 Detailed Summary of My Financial Career by Stephen 
Leacock 
My Financial Career is a humorous short story by Stephen Leacock that satirizes the fear and anxiety 
many ordinary people experience when dealing with banks and financial institutions. Written in the 
first person, the story presents the narrator's amusing yet embarrassing experience of opening a 
bank account for the first time. The narrator begins by confessing that he has always been terrified 
of banks. To him, banks are not ordinary places of business but intimidating institutions filled with 
serious-looking managers, accountants, clerks, and cashiers who seem to possess great authority. 
Even entering a bank fills him with nervousness, making him feel insignificant and out of place. 
Despite his fear, he decides to open a bank account because he has saved fifty-six dollars, which he 
believes should be deposited safely. He also plans to deposit fifty dollars every month from his salary, 
making him a potentially valuable customer. 
Upon entering the bank, the narrator is immediately overwhelmed by the formal atmosphere. 
Determined to appear confident, he approaches one of the clerks and whispers that he wishes to see 
the manager "alone." His secretive manner creates the false impression that he is an important 
businessman involved in confidential financial matters. The clerk promptly escorts him to the 
manager's private office. The manager, assuming that the visitor has urgent or sensitive business, 
politely asks him to sit down. The narrator, however, becomes increasingly nervous. He awkwardly 
announces that he has come to open an account and deposit money. Relieved that there is no crisis, 
the manager directs him back to the clerk to complete the formalities. 
The narrator hands over his fifty-six dollars to the accountant and is asked to sign the necessary 
documents. Although everything proceeds normally, his nervousness prevents him from thinking 
clearly. After opening the account, he suddenly decides to withdraw six dollars, intending to keep 
some cash with him. However, in his confusion, he accidentally writes a cheque for the entire amount 
of fifty-six dollars instead of six. When the cashier asks if he really wants all the money, the narrator, 
too embarrassed to admit his mistake, proudly replies, "Every cent of it." The cashier counts out the 
entire amount, and the narrator hurriedly stuffs the money into his pocket without checking it. 
Feeling completely humiliated, he walks stiffly towards the exit, trying to maintain his dignity. In his 
haste, he accidentally bumps into the door instead of the exit, causing further embarrassment before 
finally escaping from the bank. 
After leaving the building, the narrator resolves never to enter a bank again. Instead, he decides that 
he will keep all his money in cash in his pocket and his trousers rather than face another humiliating 
experience. The story ends with this comic resolution, emphasizing the narrator's exaggerated fear 
of financial institutions. 
The humour in My Financial Career arises primarily from the narrator's excessive nervousness, self-
consciousness, and inability to behave naturally in the formal environment of the bank. Stephen 
Leacock uses first-person narration, self-deprecating humour, situational irony, and 
exaggeration to create comedy while gently criticizing the intimidating atmosphere often 
associated with banks. The narrator's ordinary banking transaction becomes a series of increasingly 
absurd mistakes because of his anxiety rather than any real difficulty. The story illustrates how fear 
and lack of confidence can lead to embarrassing situations and how people often imagine institutions 

like banks to be much more frightening than they actually are. Through its light-hearted tone and 
universal theme, My Financial Career remains a timeless and entertaining satire on human 
insecurity, social awkwardness, and the psychological barriers that prevent people from acting with 
confidence in unfamiliar situations.

result from our own lack of confidence rather than from the actions of others.

confidence. He is intelligent enough to save money and plan his finances, yet he becomes 
helpless in the unfamiliar environment of a bank. His fear is psychological rather than

procedures, and make costly mistakes. Instead of correcting his error after writing the wrong 
amount on the cheque, he chooses to protect his pride. This decision results in further

sympathize with him because many people experience similar nervousness in unfamiliar

and a sense of humour.

and social expectations. His experiences remind readers that confidence is often more 
important than intelligence in everyday life. 
3. Discuss the themes and literary devices in My Financial Career. 
Answer: 
Stephen Leacock's My Financial Career combines humour with social criticism. The central 
theme is fear of institutions, showing how banks appear intimidating to inexperienced 
people. Another important theme is social anxiety, as the narrator worries excessively about 
making mistakes and being judged by others. 
The story also explores human insecurity. The narrator's fear prevents him from acting 
naturally and leads to unnecessary embarrassment. At the same time, the story demonstrates 
that many fears are exaggerated and exist only in the imagination. 
Leacock employs several literary devices. First-person narration allows readers to 
experience the narrator's thoughts directly. Situational irony appears when a simple banking 
transaction turns into a series of comic disasters. Exaggeration (hyperbole) intensifies the 
narrator's fear of banks, making the story more humorous. Self-deprecating humour is used 
throughout, as the narrator laughs at his own foolish behaviour. 
These literary techniques make the story entertaining while conveying the message that 
confidence and calmness are essential in dealing with unfamiliar situations.

Chapter 5 Who Can Be Called a Great Man? by B. R. Ambedkar 
Who Can Be Called a Great Man? is a thought-provoking essay by B. R. Ambedkar in which he 
examines the true meaning of greatness and challenges conventional ideas about what makes an 
individual truly great. Ambedkar argues that society often glorifies people for their power, wealth, 
military achievements, political success, or popularity, but these qualities alone do not make a 
person genuinely great. According to him, greatness should not be measured by fame or authority 
but by a person's contribution to the welfare and progress of humanity. A truly great person is one 
who dedicates his or her life to serving society, fighting injustice, and improving the lives of others, 
particularly those who are oppressed, marginalized, and deprived of their rights. 
Ambedkar explains that there is a significant difference between a famous person and a great person. 
Many individuals become famous because of their achievements in politics, war, business, or 
entertainment, but fame is often temporary and does not necessarily benefit society. True greatness, 
on the other hand, is rooted in moral character, selfless service, courage, wisdom, and commitment 
to social justice. Great individuals possess the vision to identify social problems and the 
determination to solve them. They are willing to challenge traditions, customs, and institutions that 
promote inequality and discrimination, even if doing so invites criticism or personal sacrifice. 
One of the central ideas of the essay is that greatness requires both intellectual ability and moral 
integrity. Ambedkar emphasizes that knowledge alone is insufficient if it is not guided by ethical 
principles. Similarly, good intentions without wisdom may fail to bring meaningful change. 
Therefore, a truly great leader combines intelligence with compassion, courage with humility, and 
power with responsibility. Such individuals inspire others not merely through words but through 
their actions and unwavering commitment to justice and equality. 
Ambedkar also stresses the importance of social reform as a defining characteristic of greatness. 
He believes that the highest form of leadership is not political domination but the ability to transform 
society by removing discrimination, exploitation, and injustice. Those who dedicate themselves to 
eliminating social evils such as caste discrimination, untouchability, inequality, and oppression 
deserve to be remembered as truly great. Their achievements create lasting benefits for future 
generations rather than temporary personal success. 
The essay further argues that greatness is closely linked to character and sacrifice. Truly great 
individuals often face opposition, criticism, and hardship because they challenge deeply rooted 
social beliefs and systems. However, they remain steadfast in their principles and continue working 
for the common good despite personal difficulties. Their courage to stand for truth and justice 
distinguishes them from ordinary leaders who may seek personal gain or public approval. 
Throughout the essay, Ambedkar encourages readers to adopt a more thoughtful and ethical 
standard when evaluating public figures. Instead of admiring people merely for their wealth, 
popularity, or political influence, society should honour those whose lives reflect integrity, 
compassion, equality, and service to humanity. He urges individuals, especially young people, to 
cultivate these qualities in their own lives so that they can contribute positively to society. The essay 
serves as both a philosophical reflection on leadership and a moral guide for responsible citizenship. 
The central message of Who Can Be Called a Great Man? is that true greatness lies in selfless 
service, moral courage, intellectual excellence, and the relentless pursuit of justice and 

human dignity. A great person is remembered not because of personal achievements or worldly 
success but because of the lasting positive impact they create in the lives of others. Through this 
essay, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar inspires readers to redefine greatness as a lifelong commitment to equality, 
social reform, and the betterment of humanity.

they face criticism or hardship. Their actions reflect moral courage and responsibility.

seeking personal success. Ambedkar teaches that society should admire individuals who

good. The essay encourages readers to evaluate greatness based on character and contribution

Answer: 
The essay explores several important themes. The foremost theme is true greatness through 
selfless service. Ambedkar argues that genuine greatness comes from working for the benefit

discrimination, oppression, and inequality. They work to create a society where every 
individual enjoys equal rights and opportunities.

honesty, integrity, courage, and compassion. Leadership without morality can become 
harmful.

becomes meaningful only when it serves humanity. Finally, the theme of sacrifice highlights 
that great people often endure hardship and criticism while pursuing justice and reform. 
Through these themes, Ambedkar inspires readers to value character, service, and humanity 
above fame and power. 

3. Discuss the relevance of Ambedkar's ideas on greatness in modern society. 
Answer: 
Dr. B. R. Ambedkar's ideas about greatness remain highly relevant in today's world. Modern 
society often celebrates celebrities, wealthy individuals, and powerful leaders. However, 
Ambedkar reminds us that true greatness depends on character and service rather than 
popularity. 
In a world facing problems such as inequality, discrimination, poverty, and social conflict, 
leaders with moral courage and compassion are essential. Ambedkar's emphasis on justice, 
equality, and human dignity continues to guide democratic societies. His ideas encourage 
citizens to respect those who work for education, social reform, human rights, and public 
welfare. 
The essay also teaches young people the importance of developing integrity, responsibility, 
and empathy. Instead of seeking only personal success, they should strive to contribute 
positively to society. 
Ambedkar's vision of greatness promotes inclusive leadership, ethical decision-making, and 
respect for human dignity. His message remains timeless because it encourages every 
individual to become an agent of positive social change.

Chapter 6 An Elementary School Classroom in a Slum by Stephen 
Spender 
An Elementary School Classroom in a Slum is a powerful and socially conscious poem by Stephen 
Spender that exposes the harsh realities of poverty, inequality, and social injustice experienced by 
children living in slums. The poem vividly portrays the miserable conditions in which these children 
are forced to live and study while criticizing a society that denies them equal opportunities for 
growth and development. Through striking imagery and emotional language, Spender contrasts the 
bleak world of the slum children with the bright and prosperous world enjoyed by privileged 
children, urging society to provide education and hope to every child. 
The poem opens with a description of an elementary school classroom situated in a slum. The 
children seated in the classroom are physically weak, unhealthy, and deprived of proper nutrition 
and care. Their pale faces and lifeless expressions reflect the hardships of poverty. One child is 
described as being as thin as "paper," suggesting extreme malnutrition and fragility. Another boy is 
compared to a "rat," emphasizing his stunted growth and neglected appearance. A girl sits with her 
head bent low, weighed down by illness and hopelessness. Among them is a boy whose eyes carry 
the burden of inherited poverty, symbolizing generations of suffering and deprivation. Only one 
child appears to retain some hope, dreaming about squirrels playing freely in trees and the open 
spaces beyond the slum. His imagination reflects a longing for the freedom and happiness that the 
others have never experienced. 
The poet then shifts attention to the classroom itself. The walls are decorated with maps, pictures of 
famous leaders, beautiful landscapes, and educational charts. These images represent a world of 
knowledge, beauty, prosperity, and opportunity. However, these attractive pictures have little 
meaning for the slum children because they remain trapped in a life of poverty and hopelessness. 
The maps show distant lands that the children are unlikely ever to visit, while the pictures of 
Shakespeare, buildings with domes, and scenic valleys symbolize a world completely disconnected 
from their harsh reality. Instead of opening doors to a better future, these classroom decorations 
merely highlight the vast gap between the privileged and the underprivileged. 
Spender describes the lives of the children outside the classroom as confined to narrow, dirty streets 
and overcrowded slums. Their world is limited by poverty, disease, hunger, and social neglect. The 
poet uses the image of "fog" to symbolize the uncertainty and hopelessness surrounding their lives. 
Their future appears dark and restricted, with little possibility of escaping the cycle of poverty. The 
repeated reference to "sealed" lives suggests that society has imprisoned these children within 
conditions over which they have no control. Their dreams and talents remain suppressed because 
of their economic circumstances. 
In the final stanza, the poet passionately appeals to governments, teachers, and society to transform 
the lives of these children through meaningful education. He argues that education should not 
merely involve displaying maps and pictures but should genuinely empower children by opening the 
"windows" of opportunity. The metaphor of breaking open the classroom walls symbolizes removing 
the barriers created by poverty and social inequality. Spender believes that only when these children 
are allowed to experience the wider world, receive quality education, and enjoy equal opportunities 

can they realize their full potential. He urges society to ensure that the children can "run azure on 
gold sands," suggesting freedom, happiness, and a life filled with dignity rather than deprivation. 
The poem concludes with a powerful message that history belongs only to those who actively shape 
it through knowledge, freedom, and opportunity. Children trapped in slums cannot become creators 
of history unless society first provides them with justice, education, and hope. Through vivid 
imagery, symbolism, contrast, and emotional appeal, Stephen Spender condemns social inequality 
and calls for educational reform as a means of breaking the cycle of poverty. An Elementary School 
Classroom in a Slum remains a timeless plea for equal educational opportunities and a reminder that 
every child, regardless of social background, deserves the chance to dream, learn, and build a better 
future.

Chapter 7 Fidelity by William Wordsworth 
William Wordsworth's poem "Fidelity" is a narrative poem that celebrates the unwavering loyalty 
of a dog toward its deceased master while exploring themes of love, devotion, death, and the 
emotional bond between humans and animals. Based on a true incident that reportedly occurred in 
the Scottish Highlands, the poem reflects the Romantic belief that animals possess noble emotions 
and moral virtues often comparable to or even greater than those of humans. Through vivid natural 
imagery and an emotionally moving narrative, Wordsworth presents fidelity as one of the highest 
virtues. 
The poem begins with the speaker recounting a remarkable story that has been widely told among 
the local people. A traveller is making his way through a lonely mountainous region, surrounded by 
rugged hills, valleys, and streams. As he moves through the quiet landscape, he notices a dog 
wandering alone. The animal appears restless and repeatedly returns to the same spot, as though 
trying to attract attention. Curious about the dog's unusual behaviour, the traveller decides to follow 
it. The dog's actions are not random; instead, they seem deliberate and purposeful, revealing its 
desperate attempt to communicate something important to another human being. 
The traveller soon discovers the tragic reason behind the dog's strange conduct. Hidden among the 
rocks lies the lifeless body of the dog's master, who had apparently died after suffering an accident 
in the remote mountains. The master had likely slipped or fallen while travelling through the 
dangerous terrain. Throughout the entire period following his master's death, the faithful dog had 
refused to leave the body. Instead, it remained beside its owner, guarding him day and night despite 
hunger, exhaustion, loneliness, and exposure to harsh weather. The dog's instinctive devotion 
reflects an extraordinary level of faithfulness that surpasses ordinary expectations. 
Wordsworth carefully describes the emotional relationship between the dog and its master. The 
animal's loyalty is presented not as a result of training or obligation but as an expression of genuine 
love. Even though the master can no longer provide food, protection, or companionship, the dog 
continues to perform its duty with complete dedication. This selfless commitment demonstrates that 
true affection does not depend upon personal gain or reward. The dog's behaviour becomes a 
powerful symbol of unconditional love, illustrating the Romantic ideal that sincere emotions arise 
naturally from the heart. 
Nature plays an important role throughout the poem. The lonely mountains, silent valleys, flowing 
streams, and isolated landscape create an atmosphere of solemnity and reverence. Rather than 
serving merely as a backdrop, nature reflects the emotional depth of the story. The peaceful 
surroundings contrast with the sorrow of death while also highlighting the purity of the dog's 
devotion. Wordsworth suggests that both nature and animals possess an innate goodness that 
civilized society often overlooks. The remote setting also emphasizes the vulnerability of human life 
and the enduring strength of natural affection. 
As the traveller understands the situation, he ensures that the dead man receives proper attention 
and burial. Although the master has died, the dog's loyalty gains recognition from other people, 
transforming a private act of devotion into a lasting moral example. The story survives because those 
who hear it are deeply moved by the animal's extraordinary faithfulness. Wordsworth implies that 

such examples inspire humanity to cultivate virtues such as compassion, gratitude, and 
steadfastness in their own lives. 
The poem also reflects important characteristics of the Romantic movement. Wordsworth elevates 
the ordinary lives of common people rather than focusing on kings or heroes. He presents simple 
rural life as a source of profound moral lessons. The poem emphasizes powerful emotions, reverence 
for nature, and respect for the instincts of animals. Instead of presenting philosophical arguments, 
Wordsworth allows the touching narrative itself to demonstrate that love, loyalty, and fidelity are 
universal values shared across all living beings. 
The central theme of "Fidelity" is unwavering loyalty in the face of death. The dog becomes a symbol 
of faithfulness that remains unbroken even when all hope has disappeared. The poem also explores 
themes of friendship, sacrifice, compassion, mortality, and the moral superiority of genuine affection 
over self-interest. Through the moving story of a faithful dog, Wordsworth reminds readers that love 
is measured not by words but by actions, and that true fidelity endures beyond hardship, separation, 
and even death. 
Overall, "Fidelity" is a deeply emotional narrative poem that honours the noble qualities found in 
both animals and nature. By portraying the dog's unshakable devotion to its deceased master, 
Wordsworth demonstrates that the purest forms of love are often silent, selfless, and enduring. The 
poem leaves readers with a lasting appreciation for loyalty as one of the greatest human—and 
animal—virtues, reinforcing the Romantic conviction that nature and its creatures possess profound 
moral wisdom.

emotions and moral virtues.

through the lonely Scottish mountains notices a dog behaving strangely. Curious, he follows it

stayed beside the body day and night despite hunger, loneliness, and harsh weather. The 
traveller arranges for the man's burial, and the dog's remarkable loyalty becomes widely

it refuses to leave the body. It protects and watches over the deceased owner despite suffering

through selfless actions. 
The dog's faithfulness becomes an example for humanity to follow. 
3. Explain the importance of nature in Fidelity. 
Answer: 
Nature plays an important role throughout the poem. The lonely mountains, silent valleys, 
flowing streams, and rugged landscape create an atmosphere of peace and sadness. 

Nature reflects the emotional mood of the poem while emphasizing the isolation of the dead 
master and the unwavering devotion of the dog. The natural surroundings also highlight the 
Romantic belief that nature is pure and spiritually uplifting. 
Wordsworth uses nature not simply as scenery but as a living presence that enhances the 
emotional impact of the story. 
4. How does Fidelity reflect the characteristics of Romantic poetry? 
Answer: 
The poem displays many features of Romanticism. 
● It celebrates nature. 
● It focuses on ordinary people instead of kings or heroes. 
● It values emotions over reason. 
● It presents animals as noble beings capable of deep love. 
● It teaches moral lessons through simple experiences. 
Wordsworth shows that true wisdom can be found in nature and ordinary life rather than in 
wealth or social status. 
5. Discuss the themes of Fidelity. 
Answer: 
The poem explores several important themes. 
The main theme is unwavering loyalty. The dog remains faithful even after its master's death. 
Other themes include unconditional love, sacrifice, friendship, compassion, mortality, and the 
relationship between humans and animals. 
The poem also emphasizes that genuine affection is selfless and does not seek personal 
benefit. Through the faithful dog, Wordsworth reminds readers that actions reveal true love 
more than words.

loyalty, devotion, and unconditional love. Based on a true incident from the Scottish Highlands,

day and night without expecting any reward. Its behaviour demonstrates complete

affection rather than self-interest. The poem teaches that genuine love is shown through 
sacrifice and steadfastness. Even death cannot destroy the bond between the master and the 
faithful animal. 
Nature strengthens the emotional power of the poem. The quiet mountains and valleys create 
an atmosphere of solemn beauty while reflecting the dignity of the dog's loyalty. The peaceful 
landscape contrasts with the tragedy of death, making the story even more touching. 
Ultimately, Fidelity celebrates one of the highest virtues—faithfulness. Wordsworth reminds 
readers that love is measured through actions, not words. The poem continues to inspire 
readers by showing that true devotion endures beyond hardship and even death. 
2. Examine the Romantic elements in Wordsworth's Fidelity. 
Answer: 
Fidelity is an excellent example of Romantic poetry because it reflects the major ideals of the 
Romantic Movement. 
One important Romantic feature is the celebration of nature. The poem is set in the lonely 
Scottish Highlands, where mountains, valleys, rocks, and streams create a peaceful yet solemn 
atmosphere. Nature is not merely background scenery but an active force that reflects human 
emotions. 
Another Romantic element is the emphasis on powerful emotions. Instead of focusing on 
reason or intellectual arguments, Wordsworth tells a deeply emotional story of love and 
devotion. Readers are moved by the faithful dog's behaviour rather than by philosophical 
explanations. 
The poem also values ordinary life. The characters are not kings or famous heroes but an 
ordinary traveller, a common man, and a simple dog. Wordsworth believed that ordinary 
experiences reveal universal truths about humanity. 
Animals occupy an important place in Romantic literature. In Fidelity, the dog is portrayed as 
possessing noble qualities such as loyalty, compassion, and selfless love. Wordsworth suggests 
that animals often display virtues that humans themselves should imitate. 
Finally, the poem teaches moral values through natural experience rather than formal 
instruction. The touching narrative encourages readers to appreciate loyalty, kindness, 
sacrifice, and unconditional love. 
Thus, Fidelity perfectly illustrates Romantic ideals by combining nature, emotion, simplicity, 
and moral wisdom into one unforgettable narrative. 
3. Analyse the character of the faithful dog in Fidelity. 
Answer: 

The faithful dog is the emotional centre of Wordsworth's Fidelity. Though it never speaks, its 
actions communicate deep love, devotion, and moral strength. 
After its master dies in an accident, the dog refuses to leave the body. It remains nearby 
despite hunger, cold weather, loneliness, and danger. Instead of abandoning its master, it 
faithfully guards the body until someone discovers it. 
The dog's actions are motivated entirely by love. It receives no reward because its master is 
dead, yet its loyalty remains unchanged. This makes its devotion completely selfless. The 
animal also displays intelligence by attracting the traveller's attention and leading him to the 
body. 
Wordsworth presents the dog as an example of perfect fidelity. The poet suggests that genuine 
affection is expressed through actions rather than words. The dog's behaviour becomes a 
moral lesson for humanity, encouraging people to practise loyalty, gratitude, and compassion. 
The dog also symbolizes the close bond between humans and animals. Wordsworth argues 
that animals possess noble emotions and deserve respect because they share many moral 
qualities with human beings. 
Through this memorable character, the poet celebrates unconditional love that survives even 
death. The faithful dog remains one of the finest literary symbols of loyalty in English poetry.

Chapter 8 My Mother's Saree by Vaidehi 
Vaidehi's "My Mother's Saree" is a deeply nostalgic and emotionally rich poem that celebrates a 
mother's enduring love, sacrifice, and presence through the symbolic image of her saree. The poem 
is not merely about a piece of clothing but about memory, identity, tradition, and the unbreakable 
bond between a mother and her child. The speaker reflects upon her mother's old saree, carefully 
preserved in a wooden box wrapped in white muslin cloth with mothballs. The sight of the saree 
immediately brings back vivid memories of her mother. Every fold of the fabric reflects her mother's 
disciplined nature, cleanliness, and meticulous habits. The carefully ironed pleats, the fragrance of 
camphor, incense, and aromatic roots stored with the saree all evoke the mother's personality and 
presence, making the saree seem almost alive. The speaker suggests that her mother's entire 
character—her orderliness, devotion to work, and graceful dignity—is preserved within the folds of 
the garment. 
As the poem progresses, the saree becomes a symbol of the mother's hardworking life. The poet 
remembers the familiar sounds of her mother's bangles jingling as she moved briskly about the 
house performing her daily duties. The tucked-in pleats of the saree symbolize her readiness to work 
tirelessly for her family. The broad pallu with its straight lines represents the moral strength and 
upright principles by which the mother lived her life. To the child, the saree also served practical 
purposes—it became a tool for discipline when necessary, gently correcting naughty children, while 
at the same time offering comfort and protection. Thus, the saree embodies both maternal authority 
and unconditional affection. The poet recalls the knots tied into the saree, which seemed to contain 
mysterious treasures and secrets, reflecting the hidden wisdom and experiences of motherhood. 
Even the colourful yellow Madhura saree with its green floral border reminds the speaker of a queen, 
suggesting that, in her eyes, her mother possessed the dignity, beauty, and majesty of royalty. 
The speaker then moves into memories of her childhood, when the saree seemed endless in length. 
As a little girl, she tried to measure it and wrap it around herself, but it always appeared larger than 
she imagined. This endlessness symbolizes the limitless nature of a mother's love, care, and sacrifice. 
No matter how much the child tries to comprehend it, a mother's affection always exceeds 
understanding. The saree is closely associated with the natural world and traditional rural life. 
Through references to the latex of mango and cashew trees, fragrant local flowers like Ranja, Kepala, 
and Suragi, and the golden wheat grains used during the New Year festival of Kani, the poet connects 
the mother with the cultural traditions and agricultural life of Karnataka. The saree thus becomes a 
repository of family customs, seasonal rituals, and cultural continuity, linking one generation to the 
next. 
The poem gradually shifts from joyful remembrance to quiet sorrow. The speaker recalls that her 
mother always dreamt of owning a silk saree, but by the time this modest dream was fulfilled, her 
husband—the speaker's father—had passed away. Although the mother now wears the silk saree 
she had long desired, the happiness associated with that dream has vanished because the person 
with whom she wished to share it is no longer alive. This poignant moment illustrates one of the 
poem's central truths: material possessions lose much of their meaning when personal relationships 
are broken by loss. The fulfilment of the mother's dream comes at a time when emotional fulfilment 
is impossible, highlighting the sacrifices and delayed aspirations that many women experience 
throughout their lives. 

In the concluding lines, the speaker sees her mother's old handwoven Udupi saree hanging quietly 
before her. Overcome with emotion, she unfolds it and wraps herself in it. The act is symbolic—it is 
as though she is embracing her mother's love, warmth, protection, and memory once again. Wrapped 
in the saree, she softly utters the word "Amma," a word that, despite being spoken countless times, 
never loses its freshness or emotional power. The final image suggests that although time passes and 
physical objects grow old, a mother's love remains eternal and ever-renewing. The saree becomes 
an heirloom that carries not only the mother's scent and touch but also her values, sacrifices, and 
unconditional affection across generations. 
Overall, "My Mother's Saree" is a touching tribute to motherhood and the ordinary objects that 
preserve extraordinary memories. Vaidehi transforms a simple household garment into a profound 
symbol of maternal love, cultural heritage, feminine resilience, and family history. Through vivid 
sensory imagery, emotional recollection, and rich symbolism, the poem reminds readers that the 
essence of a mother continues to live in the smallest things she leaves behind. The poem ultimately 
celebrates the timeless truth that while material objects may age, the love, care, and influence of a 
mother remain everlasting in the hearts of her children.
